hints: Focus on the exact definition of atomisation, forming one mole of gaseous atoms from the element.
Notice that iodine is a solid in its standard state at 298 K, not a gas, so your reactant must be $\text{I}_2(s)$.
Check the mole ratio needed to make exactly one mole of $\text{I}(g)$, and see what fraction of $\text{I}_2$ that requires.
walkthrough:
**Recall the definition of atomisation**

Think of atomisation as pulling an element completely apart into single, separate gas atoms. By definition it always makes exactly 1 mole of gaseous atoms.

Rule:
$$\text{element in standard state} \rightarrow 1 \text{ mol } \text{X}(g)$$

**Find the standard state of iodine**

At standard conditions iodine is a dark grey solid, so we must start from $\text{I}_2(s)$. Starting from $\text{I}_2(g)$ would already be partly atomised, because you have missed out sublimation.

So far:
$$\text{I}_2(s) \rightarrow \text{I}(g)$$

**Balance for one mole of atoms**

One $\text{I}_2$ molecule gives two $\text{I}$ atoms, but we only want one mole of $\text{I}(g)$. So we need only half a mole of $\text{I}_2(s)$.

Correct equation:
$$\frac{1}{2}\text{I}_2(s) \rightarrow \text{I}(g)$$

options.A: This has the correct 1 mole of I(g) but the wrong reactant state. I2(g) is not the standard state of iodine, so this misses the enthalpy of sublimation from solid to gas.
options.B: This is wrong twice. It starts from I2(g) instead of I2(s), and it forms 2 moles of I(g). That is the bond dissociation enthalpy of I2, not the atomisation enthalpy which must form 1 mole.
options.C: This is perfect. It starts from the standard state, I2(s), and forms exactly 1 mole of gaseous atoms, I(g). That matches the definition of standard enthalpy change of atomisation.
options.D: This starts from the correct standard state I2(s) but forms 2 moles of I(g). Atomisation must be scaled to 1 mole of gaseous atoms, so you need 1/2 I2(s), not a whole mole.
